said: 1: The sunflower turns to the sun, which is a plain fact anyone knows about sunflowers. 2: The sunflower turns to the sun and not to you: a small, dry snub that hints at being ignored or alone. why: Version 1 is a plain fact about the thing. Version 2 is a short deadpan joke with a quiet edge. The "you" is general and does not point at the reader's study.

1: The sunflower comes back every year without her, so the reader is told she is gone or soon will be. 2: She knows the flower's name, which echoes n02 (he forgets, she and the flower remember) and hints quietly at the gap between them. why: Version 1 says the loss out loud before the story is ready (she is still present in n06 and n07). Version 2 is a quiet hint built on an earlier page.

1: The fish seem to watch for someone coming, which quietly echoes "Nobody comes from there" and the far light. 2: The fish come when people come, which reads mostly as a plain fact about pond fish. why: Version 2 is close to a plain fact about the thing and uses more words. Version 1 is a short hint about waiting.
1: Every night she brings him coffee at the far light and asks nothing: quiet, steady care. 2: The same text, word for word. why: The two versions are identical.

1: A cold, windy night, and he said nothing to her about it, told in one long, padded sentence. 2: Wind on the hill, and he said nothing: short, and it echoes "Courage, in none." why: Version 1 breaks Simple English (one long sentence, many extra words) and explains too much. Version 2 says the same thing in a few plain words.

1: He now carries his own coffee and nobody asks, so the reader feels without being told that she is gone. 2: The same, plus a joke that even the rude snail does not ask. why: Version 2's snail joke pushes into the quiet moment of loss and shrinks it. That is loud whimsy at the wrong time. Version 1 shows the loss and stops.

1: He waters "your side" of the garden every morning, in a long sentence padded with detail. 2: He waters "your side" of the garden too: the same quiet sign that she is gone, in a few words. why: Version 1 breaks Simple English ("early", "the same way I always do" add words and nothing else). Version 2 says the same thing more plainly.

1: She tells him a flower's name and he repeats it, knowing he will forget it while the flower will not. 2: The same text, word for word: she names a flower, he repeats it, he will forget, the flower won't. why: Q1 same, Q2 same, Q3 same, Q4 same. The two versions are identical.

1: Tapping the sunflower shows a plain fact: it always faces the sun. 2: Tapping the sunflower shows that it faces the sun and ignores you, a small dry joke. why: Q1 2, Q2 same, Q3 2, Q4 2. Version 1 only states a known fact, so it reads like filler. "Not at you" is dry, a little rude, and close to the cat/Migas lines.

1: The sunflower thought says that she knows its name, which points back to n02, where he can't keep the names. 2: The sunflower thought says that it comes back every year without her, which hints that she will be gone. why: Q1 2, Q2 1, Q3 1, Q4 same. Version 2 pulls harder, but it is unclear: she is still here, and sunflowers don't return each year. It also gives away the loss too early and too heavily. Version 1 is quiet, clear and dry.

1: Tapping the pond shows that the fish keep watch on who is coming. 2: Tapping the pond shows that the fish come when someone comes, a plain fish habit that echoes the stand-off, where neither side goes first. why: Q1 2, Q2 2, Q3 2, Q4 same. Version 2 is concrete and simple, and it comments on n09 ("pride, on both sides") without saying so. Version 1 is vaguer and makes the fish more human.

1: He writes at length that the hill was windy and cold tonight and that he didn't tell her. 2: He notes that it was windy on the hill and that he said nothing. why: Q1 2, Q2 same, Q3 2, Q4 2. Version 1 is long, flat and explains itself, and every clause is padding. Version 2 is terse and matches "she doesn't ask" and "courage, in none".

1: He carries his own coffee up to watch the far light, nobody asks, and he jokes that the rude snail doesn't ask either. 2: He carries his own coffee up to watch the far light, and nobody asks, so she is gone. why: Q1 2, Q2 2, Q3 2, Q4 2. In Version 2 the empty place lands by itself, after d1 and d2. The snail joke in Version 1 ("the rude thing") breaks the moment and feels cute, not dry.

1: He leaves her a note: he watered her side of the garden too. 2: He leaves her a note: he went out early and watered her side too, the way he always does. why: Q1 1, Q2 same, Q3 1, Q4 1. Version 1 is short and the loss stays unsaid. Version 2 adds filler ("this morning", "the same way I always do") that explains, and it fights the "too".

1: The reader feels his gentle sense that his memory is weak and the flowers last longer than he does. 2: The same; the text is word for word the same as version 1. why: The two versions are identical, so neither breaks a rule the other keeps.

1: The reader smiles at Migas, a bold little thief, and at a quiet stand-off with the cat that nobody breaks. 2: The reader gets the same scene, but in stiff, fancy words that push them away from it. why: Version 2 breaks Simple English ("diminutive portal", "consumes", "contrition", "regards", "neither party intervenes"), and the dry joke is lost under the register. Version 1 says the same thing in plain words.

1: The reader gets a small deadpan shrug: the flower has its own focus and ignores you, which echoes "Not for me". 2: The reader learns that sunflowers face the sun. why: Version 2 is a plain fact about the thing. Version 1 is a dry joke with a light echo of the story, and it is quiet.

1: The reader feels the quiet gap again: she knows the names, and he forgets them (an echo of n02). 2: The reader senses that she is gone and that the flower comes back without her. why: Version 2 tells the loss before the story is ready, because the notes still have her alive and present. It is also odd for an annual flower. Version 1 is a quiet hint that is tied to n02.

1: The reader sees that the fish come when someone comes, a quiet mirror of the man who does not go to the far light. 2: The reader gets a light picture of fish who watch the path, as if someone is expected. why: Version 1 is close to a plain fact about fish, but its "comes / come" echoes "Nobody comes from there" and hints that one step brings the other. Version 2 is fine, but vaguer, and it assumes a visitor. The gap is small.

1: The reader learns that it was windy and cold, and that he kept quiet about it to her. 2: The reader feels a short, closed silence on the hill, and it is open what he did not say. why: Version 1 breaks Simple English: one long, padded sentence that explains what he did not say and to whom. Version 2 says it in six plain words and leaves the silence open.

1: The reader sees that the coffee and the question are gone, and understands without being told that she is gone. 2: The reader is told plainly that she died in the spring. why: Version 2 breaks "shown, never said" because it states the death. Version 1 shows the loss through the coffee and "Nobody asks", which echo d1 and d2.

1: The reader feels that he still keeps her side of the garden, in a long, routine-heavy sentence. 2: The reader feels the same thing in one short line that speaks to her. why: Version 1 breaks Simple English. "This morning I went out early" and "the same way I always do" add words but no meaning. Version 2 says the same thing in fewer, plainer words.

1: She tells him a flower's name, he repeats it, and he knows he will forget it while the flower won't. 2: The same lines as version 1, word for word. why: The two versions are the same text, so all four answers are "same".

1: The sunflower thought only notes that it always faces the sun. 2: The sunflower faces the sun and not the person looking at it. why: Q1 2 (the small turn has some life); Q2 same (both plain); Q3 2 (dry, matches the looking motif with Migas and the cat, without explaining); Q4 2 (version 1 reads like a fact-card filler, version 2's second half earns its place).

1: The sunflower thought says she knows its name, which he still doesn't. 2: The sunflower thought says it comes back every year without her. why: Q1 2 ("without her" is a strong hook); Q2 1 ("without her" is unclear here, since she is still clearly there in the notes); Q3 1 (version 2 hints at loss too early and leans sentimental, and a sunflower does not come back each year); Q4 1 (quiet callback to n02, each word earns its place).
1: He watches the far light at night, she brings him coffee and does not ask. 2: The same lines as version 1, word for word. why: The two versions are the same text, so all four answers are "same".

1: The pond thought says the fish watch for whoever is coming. 2: The pond thought says the fish come up because they are looking for someone. why: Q1 1 ("who's coming" hints at a visitor and ties to the far light); Q2 2 (the fish coming up is a concrete action); Q3 1 (drier, shorter, while "looking for someone" leans toward sad); Q4 same (both short and both earn their place).

1: He takes his own coffee up the hill, nobody asks, and he jokes that not even the rude snail asks. 2: He takes his own coffee up the hill alone and nobody asks. why: Q1 2 (the bare change from "She brings" to "I bring my own" leaves a silence that pulls); Q2 2 (the absence lands cleanly, while the snail joke blurs it); Q3 2 ("the rude thing" is cute and softens the moment); Q4 2 (the snail clause feels like extra padding).

1: There is less water each morning, and the line explains that the mouse drinks it, so the care goes on. 2: There is less water each morning. why: Q1 2 (the line leaves something to wonder about); Q2 1 (it says who drinks it); Q3 2 (version 1 explains and states the feeling outright with "so the care goes on", and calls Migas "the mouse"); Q4 2 (version 1's second sentence is explanation, not a line worth reading for itself).

1: The narrator finds a small door in the hedge for Migas, who eats their bread, and Migas and the cat just stare at each other. It is told in long, formal words ("diminutive portal", "contrition"). 2: The same scene in plain words: a little door for Migas, who eats their bread and never says sorry, and a cat and Migas who stare and do nothing. why: 1: 2, the plain version keeps the joke, and the long words in 1 bury it. 2: 2, a learner can read every word. 3: 2, the formal words in 1 break the dry, quiet voice. 4: in 2 every line counts; in 1 the wording itself gets in the way.

1: They used to walk to the end of the garden every evening and she jumped the stile, but now brambles taller than him block the way. 2: Every evening they walk to the end of the garden, she jumps the stile, he goes slowly, and she teases that the brambles are faster than him. why: 1: 1, the change to past tense ("Before... Now") quietly suggests something has changed and makes you wonder about her. 2: 1, "brambles are faster than me" in 2 takes a second read. 3: 1 is dry and leaves out the reason; 2 is dry with gentle humour, so roughly even. 4: in 1 every line counts; the last line of 2 is a little puzzling.

1: The sunflower thought says she knows its name. 2: The same thought, in very formal words ("cognizant of its nomenclature"). why: 1: 1, it echoes n02 (she tells him the flower names) and hits gently. 2: 1, plain words. 3: 1, the formal words in 2 break the voice completely. 4: 1 is one clean line; 2 is word-play that gets in the way.

1: The fish rise in the pond as if looking for someone. 2: The fish watch whoever is coming. why: 1: 1, "looking for someone" hints at an absence without saying it. 2: 1, "watch who's coming" in 2 reads a little awkwardly. 3: both are quiet; 1 comes slightly closer to feeling but does not tip over. 4: both are single, short lines; 1 carries more.
1: Tonight the far light is on as always, she brings him coffee on the hill and asks nothing. 2: Word for word the same as version 1. why: The two versions are the same, so every question is "same".

1: The far light is on as always, but now he carries his own coffee up and nobody asks, so she is gone without it being said. 2: The far light is on as always; she died in the spring, and he brings his own coffee now. why: 1: 1, "Nobody asks" echoing "She doesn't ask" lands harder because the reader puts it together. 2: 2, it says outright that she died. 3: 1, 2 explains the loss, and the voice never explains. 4: in 1 every line counts; "She died in the spring" in 2 does the reader's work for them.

1: Two cups on the table, one stays empty, and he leaves it by the little door with water for Migas; Rayo the snail listens to him and never says no. 2: The same, plus "He's a snail. What would he say? Ha." why: 1: 1, the man who disliked snails now talking to one is touching on its own. 2: same, both are clear. 3: 1, the extra line in 2 explains the joke and laughs at it. 4: the last added sentences in 2 are filler.

1: Each morning there is less water by the little door, because the mouse drinks it, "so the care goes on." 2: Each morning there is less water. why: 1: 2, the bare line leaves a small mystery to come back to. 2: 1, it says who drinks the water; from this file alone, 2's water has no clear source. 3: 2, "so the care goes on" explains the feeling and is sentimental. 4: the second sentence of 1 explains what the first only hints at.

1: The reader feels how short his memory is next to hers and the flower's: he repeats the name, will lose it, and the flower keeps it. 2: Same text, same effect: a quiet, wry sense that he forgets and the flower does not. why: The two versions are word for word the same.

1: The reader smiles at a little door, a cheeky Migas who takes their bread, and a calm stand-off with the cat. 2: The reader gets the same scene, but in stiff, fancy words ("diminutive portal", "contrition", "neither party intervenes") that kill the dry tone. why: 2 breaks Simple English with rare, formal words that many learners won't know. 1 says the same thing in plain words.

1: The reader learns early that the shared walk is over ("before... now there are brambles") and feels that she is gone or that something ended. 2: The reader sees a living routine: she jumps the stile, he goes slowly, and she teases that the brambles are faster than him. why: 1 shows the loss too soon, in the fifth note, while every other note still has her present, and "Before," at the start reads stiffly. 2 stays in the present, plants the brambles, and has a dry joke in her voice.

1: The reader links the sunflower back to her teaching flower names: she knows it, he does not. 2: The reader gets the same hint, but wrapped in heavy words ("cognizant of its nomenclature"). why: 2 breaks Simple English badly. 1 is short and plain, and it quietly points back to n02.

1: The reader senses that the pond is waiting too, watching for someone to come, maybe the far light. 2: The reader is told the fish are looking for someone, which spells out absence and longing. why: 2 is wordier and nearly names the feeling ("looking for someone"). 1 is shorter, more deadpan, and leaves it open.

1: The reader is told flat out that she died in the spring, and that he now carries his own coffee. 2: The reader feels her absence only because the pattern breaks: he brings his own coffee, and "nobody asks." why: 1 breaks "shown, never said" by stating the death. 2 shows it through the broken ritual, which is much stronger.

1: The reader feels his loneliness: an empty cup left out for Migas, and a snail he talks to. Then a joke that explains itself ("He's a snail. What would he say? Ha."). 2: The reader gets the same loneliness, and it ends on the dry "He never says no." why: 1's extra line nudges the reader and spells out its own joke, so it breaks "whimsy is quiet." 2 stops at the deadpan line and lets the reader do the rest.

1: The reader is told the mouse drinks the water and that "the care goes on", so the meaning is explained. 2: The reader sees only that there is less water each morning by the door and is left to wonder. why: 1 explains what the thing means (and names Migas as a mouse), which breaks "shown, never said." 2 is a quiet hint, even if it is a little cryptic here.

1: The reader feels the evening walks with her are over: the path is lost to brambles, and something has happened to her. 2: The reader sees a fond daily walk, her quick and him slow, with a dry hint that the brambles are winning. why: 1 jumps to "Before... Now" and points at her loss while every earlier note still has her here, so it tells the turn too early. 2 stays in the present, uses plainer words, and hides its hint in a quiet joke in her voice.

1: The sunflower points back to her. She knows the names he forgets. 2: Same idea, but in big, stiff words most learners cannot read. why: 2 badly breaks Simple English, and the stiff wording is a joke that does not land. 1 is a quiet callback to n02.
1: She brings him coffee on the hill and does not ask about the light. 2: Identical to 1. why: The two versions are word for word the same.

1: The fish seem to wait for a visitor, a quiet hint that someone may come. 2: The fish rise and seem to search for someone, a hint that someone is missing. why: Both are quiet hints. 1 says it in fewer words and stays drier. 2 opens with a plain fact about the fish and pushes the meaning harder.

1: She is no longer on the hill and he drinks alone, then a joke about a rude snail breaks the moment. 2: She is no longer on the hill. He brings his own coffee, and the silence carries the loss. why: 1's snail joke is loud whimsy that undercuts the beat. 2 shows the loss and stops.

1: Something drinks the water by the little door, and the line tells us this means her care goes on. 2: Each morning the water by the little door is lower, so something small still comes. why: 1 says what it means ("so the care goes on") and names the drinker, which explains. 2 shows it and lets the reader make the link.

1: He leaves her empty cup for Migas and talks to a snail, then laughs at his own joke. 2: He leaves her empty cup for Migas and talks to a snail that never says no. He is lonely. why: 1's "He's a snail. What would he say? Ha." explains its own joke and nudges the reader. 2 stops while the line still has weight.

1: In stiff, over-formal words, he says there is a small door in the hedge for Migas, who eats their bread without saying sorry, and the cat and Migas just stare at each other. 2: In plain words, he says there is a little door in the hedge for Migas, who eats their bread and never says sorry, and the cat and Migas only look at each other. why: Q1 2, Q2 2, Q3 2, Q4 2. Version 1's "diminutive portal", "expresses contrition" and "neither party intervenes" break the plain voice of n01–n03 and make it hard for a learner. Version 2 says the same thing with dry timing.

1: Every evening they used to walk to the end of the garden, she jumped the stile and he went slowly, and now brambles taller than him block the way. 2: Every evening they walk to the end of the garden, she jumps the stile and he goes slowly, and she teases him that the brambles are faster than he is. why: Q1 1 (the "Before… Now" turn is a quiet hook), Q2 1 (an overgrown path is clear, while "faster than me" makes you stop and work it out), Q3 same, Q4 same. Version 2 keeps her in the present like n01–n04 and is warmer. Version 1 hints at a change without explaining it, and its brambles match the real barrier in the garden.

1: Tapping the sunflower gives "She is cognizant of its nomenclature." 2: Tapping the sunflower gives "She knows its name." why: Q1 2, Q2 2, Q3 2, Q4 2. Version 2 echoes n02 (she tells him flower names) in four plain words. Version 1 uses Latinate words that are wrong for this voice and opaque to a learner.

1: Tapping the pond says the fish come up whenever someone comes. 2: Tapping the pond says the fish watch who is coming. why: Q1 2 (a slight sense that someone is expected, after n09), Q2 1, Q3 1 (a plain observation with neat parallel words, no personifying), Q4 same. Both are one good line. Version 1 is drier and grows quietly from "There's a fish. Or two."

1: He writes at length that it was windy and cold on the hill tonight but he did not tell her. 2: He notes the wind on the hill and that he said nothing. why: Q1 2, Q2 1 (it spells out what he kept quiet and from whom), Q3 2, Q4 2 (version 1 is padded). Version 2's "I said nothing" matches "She doesn't ask" and his lack of courage. Version 1's "about it to her" makes the silence small.

1: The far light is there as always, he says plainly that she died in the spring, and he brings his own coffee up now. 2: The far light is there as always, he brings his own coffee up, and nobody asks. why: Q1 2, Q2 1, Q3 2, Q4 same. "Nobody asks" reverses "She doesn't ask" and shows she is gone without saying it. Version 1 states the death outright, which is clearer but explains what the story should let the reader find.

1: He tells her that early this morning he went out and watered her side of the garden too, the same way he always does. 2: He tells her he watered her side of the garden too. why: Q1 2, Q2 same, Q3 2, Q4 2. Version 1's "this morning I went out early" and "the same way I always do" are filler and weaken the bare "your side… too", which echoes "Two sides. Hers wins."

1: There are two cups and one stays empty, he leaves it with water by the little door for Migas, and he talks to Rayo the snail, who never says no. 2: The same, but he adds a joke that a snail could not say anything anyway: "Ha." why: Q1 1, Q2 same, Q3 1, Q4 1 (the added "He's a snail. What would he say? Ha." explains the joke and is filler). Version 1 lets the snail line sit, after "I don't like snails".

1: She says a flower's name, he repeats it, and he expects to forget it while the flower keeps it, all in stiff, old-fashioned words ("enunciates the appellation", "the morrow"). 2: She tells him a flower's name, he says it too, and he knows he will forget it tomorrow but the flower won't. why: Version 2 wins all four questions. It says the same thing in plain words that fit the dry voice and a learner can read. Version 1's archaic wording is out of voice and gets in the way of the meaning.

1: He climbs the hill and sees a yellow light that never goes out, and the note explains that she doesn't ask because she knows it is his old friend. 2: He climbs the hill and sees a yellow light that never goes out, and she doesn't ask. why: Version 2 keeps the mystery, so it pulls the learner back, and it does not explain. The "because she knows it is my old friend" clause in Version 1 explains, gives away the later reveal, and is the only line that feels like filler. Both are equally clear about the scene.

1: She tells him his stool is too low, and he says maybe. 2: She tells him his stool is too low, and he says maybe. why: The texts are word-for-word the same, so every question gets "same". Both turn her old chair joke around.

1: He says she is gone, that he watered her side of the garden too, and that love is a little water every day. 2: He says he watered her side of the garden too. why: Version 2 lets "your side" and the empty coffee lines before it carry the loss. Version 1 states the loss ("You are gone") and adds a greeting-card moral, which is sentimental and explains. Version 1 is a little clearer in plain terms, but Version 2 is clear enough, better in voice, and makes the reader want to know more.

1: Tapping the sundial gives "The sun tells the time." 2: Tapping the sundial gives "Nobody checks the time anymore." why: Version 1 is a flat fact that adds nothing, so it is filler. Version 2 echoes "Nobody asks" and quietly shows that someone is missing, without saying so.

1: He flashes his light once in the night, and the far light does nothing. 2: He flashes his light once in the night, and "nobody did anything". why: Version 1 is clearer: the far light did not answer. Version 2 nicely echoes the cat-and-Migas standoff, but "nobody did anything" right after he did something is unclear and a little self-contradictory. Both are dry and in voice.

1: After the far light answers, the hills get a new thought: "Someone lives on the other side." 2: The hills get no new thought, so the old line stays. why: Version 1 turns the earlier "Nobody comes from there" around, the way the bench and sundial thoughts changed after events, so the world reacts. It is a little close to stating what we already know. Version 2 is restrained, but nothing new happens for the learner who taps the hills.

1: The frog gets a new line before its usual last line: "I'm not a prince." 2: The frog says its old lines as before. why: "I'm not a prince" repeats the joke the frog already made ("No kisses, please. Those stories aren't true."), so it is filler. Version 2 avoids saying the gag twice. Both are equally clear and dry.

1: The frog gets a new line before its usual last line: "No kisses, please. Those stories aren't true." 2: The frog only croaks and says "I have no more words." as before. why: Version 1 adds a small, dry, discoverable joke that rewards tapping, which is the kind of quiet whimsy that makes the frog worth visiting again. Version 2 gives nothing new. Both are clear.

1: Tapping the flower bed gives the thought "Two sides. Hers wins.", which echoes the low-chair argument. 2: Exactly the same line as version 1. why: Q1 same, Q2 same, Q3 same, Q4 same. The two texts are word for word the same.

1: The stool is worn smooth because someone sat on it for many nights, and the line says so in full with "because". 2: The stool is "Worn smooth. Many nights.", and the reader is left to work out who sat there. why: Q1 2, Q2 1, Q3 2, Q4 2. Version 1 explains, and "many, many" pads it. Version 2 says the same thing in four words, in the voice.

1: The moon is "On time again", a dry nod to the nightly watch. 2: The same line plus "Unlike some people I could name", a wink that turns it into a joke. why: Q1 1, Q2 same, Q3 1, Q4 1. The extra sentence in version 2 is arch and pokes at the reader. It is filler that breaks the quiet just as she starts to stay.

1: "Nobody checks the time anymore": a quiet line that matches d3, where she is gone and "Nobody asks". 2: The same line plus "The sundial is thrilled", which turns the absence into a joke. why: Q1 1, Q2 1, Q3 1, Q4 1. Right after d3, the joke undercuts the first hint that she is gone. Version 1 lets that weight stand.

1: "She looked at it every morning": the past tense quietly says she is no longer there. 2: "Its face looks at the path": the sunflower turns from the sun toward the path, as if it waits for someone. why: Q1 1, Q2 1, Q3 same, Q4 same. Both are good. The tense change in version 1 is a clear, unexplained blow that fits d3. Version 2 is more oblique, and "its face" is harder for a learner.

1: "Someone habitually occupied this seat each evening": the same fact in stiff, formal words. 2: "Someone sat here every evening": plain and short. why: Q1 2, Q2 2, Q3 2, Q4 2. Version 1 is not simple English, and its register does not match any other line. Version 2 says the same thing cleanly.

1: He makes two signals, the far light answers with two, and nobody has crossed the valley yet. Words like "finally", "very carefully", "between us" and "Not yet, anyway" pad it. 2: The same events in three bare lines, ending "Yet." why: Q1 2, Q2 same, Q3 2, Q4 2. Each extra word in version 1 explains or adds feeling. In version 2, "Yet." alone does the work, and it echoes "Me neither. Yet." from n03.

1: He hands the garden to the reader: learn every flower's name, slowly like Rayo, and snails are no reason. 2: He hands the garden to the reader: water both sides, slowly like Rayo, and snails are no reason. why: Q1 same, Q2 same, Q3 same, Q4 1. Both call back to earlier notes. "Learn the name of every flower" closes the loop with n02 and the learner's own task, and "slowly" fits learning better than watering.

1: He hands the garden to the reader: leave water for Migas, send two signals at night (the far light always answers), and snails are no reason. 2: The same, plus "Water both sides", which keeps her half of the garden in his last wishes. why: Q1 2, Q2 same, Q3 same, Q4 2. "Water both sides" is not filler: it carries her into the ending without saying her name. Version 1 is tighter but drops her.

1: She says a flower's name, he repeats it, and he knows he will forget it, but the flower won't. It is written in stiff, old-fashioned words ("enunciates the appellation", "morrow"). 2: She tells him a flower's name, he says it too, and he knows that tomorrow he won't know it, but the flower will. why: Q1 2, Q2 2, Q3 2, Q4 2. Version 1's archaic words are wrong for this voice and hard for a learner. Version 2 is plain and dry, and every line counts.

1: Tapping the stool shows a short thought: it is worn smooth from many nights. 2: Tapping the stool shows a long thought: the wood is worn smooth because someone sat there for many, many nights. why: Q1 1, Q2 2, Q3 1, Q4 1. Version 2 is a little clearer, but its "because someone sat here" explains, and "many, many" is padding. Version 1 has the same fact and leaves the reader to fill in the rest.

1: The moon is on time again. 2: The moon is on time again, and then comes a jab at "some people" who are not on time. why: Q1 1, Q2 1, Q3 1, Q4 1. "Unlike some people I could name" is a sitcom cliché. It breaks the quiet, dry tone, and it is not clear who it means.
1: She says his stool is too low, and he says maybe. 2: The same as version 1, word for word. why: Q1 same, Q2 same, Q3 same, Q4 same. The texts are identical.

1: He leaves a note saying he watered her side of the garden too, so the loss shows only by what he does. 2: He says she is gone, that he watered her side too, and that love is a little water every day. why: Q1 1, Q2 2, Q3 1, Q4 1. Version 2 states the loss outright and adds a greeting-card moral, which is sentimental and explaining. Version 1's one line carries all of it, and quietly.

1: Nobody checks the time anymore, and the sundial is thrilled about it. 2: Nobody checks the time anymore. why: Q1 2, Q2 same, Q3 2, Q4 2. Right after she is gone, the plain line hits hard. "The sundial is thrilled" is a loud joke that undercuts it and reads as tacked on.
